title: What is the difference between RDS Multi-AZ (synchronous standby for high availability/failover) and read replicas (asynchronous, for read scaling)?
keyPoints: Multi-AZ is a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone for automatic failover and high availability, not for read scaling.
Read replicas are asynchronous copies for scaling read throughput by offloading reads from the primary.
Multi-AZ failover is automatic and transparent on the same endpoint; read replica promotion is manual and breaks replication.
Because replicas are asynchronous, read-after-write consistency must come from the primary, not from a replica.
Production databases typically use both: Multi-AZ for availability and read replicas for read scaling.
Aurora blurs this line by offering replicas that are both readable and fast-failover targets.

s1_definition.oneliner: Multi-AZ is a hidden synchronous twin for automatic failover and availability, while read replicas are asynchronous copies you read from to scale read traffic.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Multi-AZ** – provisions a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone; every committed write is replicated before acknowledgment, and RDS fails over automatically on primary failure.
- **Read replica** – an asynchronous copy that accepts read-only queries to offload reads from the primary; replication lag means data may be slightly behind.
- **Failover behavior** – Multi-AZ failover is automatic on the same endpoint in one to two minutes; a read replica must be manually promoted, which breaks its replication link.
- **Use together** – production databases use both: Multi-AZ for availability, read replicas for read scaling.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the main ledger at National Bank of India. Multi-AZ is like having a second clerk in another branch who writes down every single transaction at the exact same moment as the main clerk, so if the main clerk suddenly leaves, the second clerk instantly becomes the main clerk with an identical, up-to-the-second ledger -- but customers never go to that second clerk for answers. A read replica is different: it is like photocopying the ledger every few seconds and placing the copies in several reading rooms, so many people who only want to read can do so without crowding the main clerk, accepting that a copy might be a few seconds behind.

```text
          RDS Multi-AZ (Synchronous Standby)

  ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐
  │   Primary (AZ-a) │ sync    │  Standby (AZ-b)  │
  │                  │────────→│                  │
  │ Writes + Reads   │ write   │  NOT readable    │
  │                  │ ack'd   │  Takes over on   │
  │ nbi-ledger.rds   │ after   │  primary failure │
  │ .amazonaws.com   │ BOTH    │                  │
  └────────┬─────────┘ persist └──────────────────┘
           │                         ▲
           │                         │ automatic
           │         failover:       │ DNS flip
           │         same endpoint ──┘
           │         1-2 minutes
           ▼         zero data loss
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │   Application    │
  │  (single endpoint│
  │   for R + W)     │
  └──────────────────┘


          RDS Read Replicas (Asynchronous Copy)

  ┌──────────────────┐  async   ┌──────────────────┐
  │   Primary        │─────────→│  Read Replica 1  │
  │ (writes + critical│  lag    │  (reports,       │
  │  reads)          │         │   dashboards)    │
  └──────────────────┘         └──────────────────┘
           │            async   ┌──────────────────┐
           └───────────────────→│  Read Replica 2  │
                                │  (analytics)     │
                                └──────────────────┘

  Application routes:
    WRITE + read-after-write  →  Primary endpoint
    Heavy read-only traffic   →  Reader endpoint
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
RDS Multi-AZ and read replicas solve two completely different problems. Multi-AZ is about availability. When I enable it, RDS keeps a synchronous standby in a second Availability Zone, and every committed write goes to both the primary and the standby before it is acknowledged, so the standby is always perfectly current. That standby is not readable -- it exists only to take over. If the primary fails, RDS automatically fails over to the standby behind the same endpoint in a minute or two with zero data loss.

Read replicas are about performance, specifically scaling reads. A read replica is a separate, readable instance that receives changes asynchronously from the primary, so it can be slightly behind. I point heavy read-only traffic like reports and dashboards at the replica's endpoint so the primary is left free for writes and latency-sensitive reads. A read replica does not fail over automatically; promoting it is a deliberate manual action that breaks its replication link.

The contrast that matters most is the failover behavior and the consistency guarantee. Multi-AZ failover is automatic and transparent on the same endpoint. Read replica promotion is manual. And because replicas are asynchronous, I must never serve a read-after-write from a replica when the value must be perfectly current -- if I just updated a balance, I read that from the primary.

At National Bank of India I ran the ledger with both features together. Multi-AZ gave me automatic failover so an Availability Zone outage promoted the synchronous standby in about ninety seconds with zero data loss. Two read replicas absorbed the month-end reporting load so live transfers stayed fast. I explicitly routed consistency-critical reads to the primary, because once a developer read a just-updated balance from a lagging replica and saw a stale value.

Remember one sentence: Multi-AZ is a synchronous hidden standby for automatic failover with zero data loss, read replicas are asynchronous copies for read scaling, and production databases use both together.
